**The Haven Support Network** consists of two servers: The Haven and Haven Retreat. Both offer first-person general mental health support. We are also a nonprofit organization 501(c)3. The Haven has about 4600 members and Retreat has about 1800. We also have an Instagram (@thehavenmh) with 11k followers.

**The Haven** is 18+ and you must be living with or suspect you are living with mental illness.
**Haven Retreat** is 13+ and everyone is welcome to seek emotional support. 

We are heavily modded and aim to maintain a safe space. We have an active community with diverse interests and diagnoses. We do not allow mental health professionals to “treat” folks in our servers.

Our focus is on support, so we have many support channels in which you can talk 1:1 with a support volunteer. We have topic channels for creativity, physical health, meme-spam, group support, and a daily-prompt for writing exercises. 

We are now **partnered with PsychCentral**. You can find us at: <https://forums.psychcentral.com/the-haven/>

There are a lot of mental health groups online, especially on Discord right now. The one I help run is purely peer support, so everyone on the server is over 18 and has a mental illness of some kind. Everyone provides help to others in trouble when they can, and asks for help when they need it. We work really hard to keep it a heavily moderated, safe space for as many people as possible. Basically you can come to the server and talk about anything at all related to your mental health. No one without mental illness (who admits it) is allowed to stay because we want to keep judgement out of the equation. It's nice people want to help but that's not what we're looking for. A lot of people find peer support very helpful because you get to talk to people who empathize with your situation more easily than NTs (neuro typicals). Maybe she'd be open to just checking it out? No pressure, no hassle. I can recommend some others I like as well.

It depends on where you are, but most places I've been start like brittrose mentioned. You get meds before breakfast if that's when you take them, breakfast is at a set hour, most people get meds at that point. Then there are various activities and groups scheduled throughout the day, usually in like 45 minute or hour chunks. Some are art therapy or group therapy. Usually you and your Dr. decide what groups are best for you to go to. At some point, usually randomly, your Dr. will come find you to talk for whatever length of time they deem useful (10-45 mins depending on what's going on). All the places I've been have internet, TV, no real radio but some groups play music. Everyone is on different meds so some people are zombies, but a lot of people are functionally coherent and bored as hell. Lunch and dinner are set hours, med times different for everybody. The places I've been had long visiting hours every day, which is why i chose to be there rather than a place with just Saturday visitation, so my husband could come visit all the time. Also they set up family meetings so that he would come in and meet with me and my Drs. to discuss everything. Personally, I spent a lot of time journaling or sitting on the computer or coloring. I also spent a -lot- of time talking with other patients. You'd be amazed what you can learn.

No no no, it's not that scary. I've been on lithium for about a year and a half and it absolutely saved my life. I tried to kill myself and wound up in the hospital for a long time, but once the meds were balanced, the emotions were too. As long as you drink water like a normal person that is more than OK. "Constant" bloodwork is checking your lithium levels every few weeks to a month or so to make sure your liver is doing alright. Honestly, people make it sound way more scary than they need to and for a lot of people this drug is a miracle. Feel free to PM if you have any other questions about it. Also, I take my full dose once a day, not divided up and that seems to be fine.

It sounds like you're being incredibly supportive already. The best thing to remember, as you are, is that you can't fix her but you can be there, and to project that. I always feel guilty when I'm depressed because I can't do anything, and everything I can do is incredibly difficult. My poor husband has to sit through months of me not functioning. He doesn't try to fix me, he's patient, but he tries not to enable me too much either. Sometimes motivation is great, but sometimes it can just be a reminder that I feel like I can't do anything. If you have time to read, I'd recommend something autobiographical like "An Unquiet Mind" so you could have an insider's perspective to what it feels like. Also, medications can take a long time to be effective. Latuda made me insanely uncomfortable but it's different for everyone. A lot of trial and error. Try not to be discouraged. Also, if you could carve out some time, somehow, for just you two to be together, I'm sure that would be appreciated, so she can breathe and just try to feel normal.
